items.stem: Consider the quotation at the start of the chapter discuss in several groups. Compare your observations and conclusions on what Kautilya recommends for a kingdom. Is it very different today?
items.answer:  Kautilya recommends that a kingdom should have fortified capitals and frontiers, be self-sustaining with fertile land, resources like mines and forests, good water supply (not solely rain-dependent), good roads/waterways, and a productive, diverse economy. Many of these principles, such as national security, resource management, infrastructure, and economic stability, are still fundamental concerns for governments today.

items.stem: How were rulers chosen in early Vedic society ?
items.answer:  In some mahajanapadas (monarchies), the raja’s position was hereditary. In others, like the ganas or sanghas (e.g., Vajji), the raja and key decisions were made by an assembly (sabha or samiti), possibly through discussion and vote, representing an early democratic form.

items.answer:  A historian would use : (i) Archaeological sources : Excavated city ruins (fortifications, structures), artifacts (pottery, Downloaded from www.pdf.tube CH 04: New Beginnings : Cities and States tools, coins like punch-marked coins) to understand urban planning, technology, daily life, and trade. (ii) Literary sources : Late Vedic texts, Buddhist and Jain literature which describe these urban centers, their governance, social structure, and economic activities, providing names of mahajanapadas and rulers.

items.stem: Why was the development of iron metallurgy so important for the growth of urbanism in the 1st millennium BCE? You may use points from the chapter but also from your knowledge or imagination.
items.answer:  Iron metallurgy was crucial because :

items.stem: What is the ‘Second Urbanisation of India’ primarily referred to as? glory

options.label: A
options.text: The re-establishment of Harappan cities’ old

options.label: B
options.text: The growth of new cities in medieval

options.label: C
options.text: A new phase of urban growth mainly

options.label: D
options.text: The development of port cities for trade

items.answer:  (C) A new phase of urban growth mainly The ‘Second Urbanisation’ denotes a significant new phase of city development that began in the 1st millennium BCE, particularly in the Ganga plains and surrounding regions, following the decline of the earlier Indus Valley Civilization.

items.stem: Which of these was NOT a primary component of the Harappan urban order that disappeared during its disintegration?

options.label: A
options.text: Elaborate public and many private structures

options.label: B
options.text: A widely used system of iron tools

items.answer:  (B) A widely used system of iron tools The Harappan civilization was known for its bronze metallurgy; widespread use of iron tools became a feature of the later Second Urbanisation. Elaborate structures, specialized occupations, and sanitation systems were hallmarks of Harappan cities.

items.stem: Archaeological excavations and ancient literature are the two main sources for understanding the Second Urbanisation. Which types of ancient literature provide these references? Mesopotamian clay tablet inscriptions

options.label: A
options.text: Only Greek and Roman historical accounts

options.label: C
options.text: Late Vedic, Buddhist, and Jain texts mainly

options.label: D
options.text: Egyptian hieroglyphic scrolls and old carvings

items.answer:  (C) Late Vedic, Buddhist, and Jain texts mainly Ancient Indian texts, including late Vedic literature, as well as Buddhist and Jain scriptures, are rich sources of information, frequently mentioning the new urban centers that emerged during the Second Urbanisation.

items.stem: What does the Sanskrit word ‘janapada’ literally mean?

options.label: A
options.text: The king’s royal palace or his court

options.label: B
options.text: A fortified city with very strong walls

options.label: D
options.text: A sacred river flowing through the land

items.answer:  (C) Where people (jana) have set foot (pada) ‘Janapada’ is a Sanskrit term where ‘jana’ means people or clan, and ‘pada’ means foot. It signifies a territory where a particular clan or group of people had settled down and established their footing.

items.stem: By the 8th or 7th centuries BCE, some early janapadas merged to form larger units known as what?
items.answer:  (C) Mahajanapadas (great territories) NODIA As janapadas grew and trade networks expanded, some merged, forming larger and more powerful political units. These larger entities were known as mahajanapadas, meaning ‘great janapadas’ or large territories.

items.stem: What was a key difference in the political system of mahajanapadas like Vajji and Malla compared to monarchies like Magadha? power raja council

options.label: A
options.text: Vajji and Malla were ruled by foreign kings

options.label: B
options.text: Vajji and Malla had assemblies with more

options.label: C
options.text: Monarchies like Magadha had no system of

options.label: D
options.text: Monarchies like Magadha had no advisory

items.answer:  (B) Vajji and Malla had assemblies with more power Unlike monarchies such as Magadha where the raja held ultimate authority, mahajanapadas like Vajji and Malla, called ganas or sanghas, had assemblies (sabha or samiti) that wielded more power, including selecting the raja and making decisions.

items.stem: The concentration of many mahajanapadas in the Ganga plains was due to several factors. Which of these was a significant reason? attacks

options.label: B
options.text: The dry climate being ideal for storage

options.label: C
options.text: The growth of agriculture in fertile plains

options.label: D
options.text: The absence of any major river systems

items.answer:  (C) The growth of agriculture in fertile plains The fertile alluvial soil of the Ganga plains supported robust agricultural growth. This agricultural surplus was a key factor in the rise and sustenance of populous states and urban centers like the mahajanapadas.

items.stem: Most capitals of the mahajanapadas were well- fortified. What defensive feature often ran outside these fortifications?
items.answer:  (C) A deep, wide moat filled To enhance their defense, the fortified capitals of most mahajanapadas were typically surrounded by a moat. This deep, wide ditch, often filled with water, served as an additional obstacle for attackers.

items.stem: If a mahajanapada was described as a ‘gana’ or ‘sangha’, what did this imply about its system of governance? assembly rule priests organization

options.label: A
options.text: It was ruled by a single, hereditary king

options.label: C
options.text: It was a territory controlled by religious

options.label: D
options.text: It was primarily a military-controlled state

items.answer:  (B) It functioned more democratically with assembly rule Mahajanapadas termed ‘ganas’ or ‘sanghas’, like Vajji, were not monarchies. Their governance was more democratic, with assemblies holding significant power in decision-making and even in the selection of the ruler, thus being called early republics.

items.stem: A major technological shift during the Second Urbanisation involved the widespread use of _____ metallurgy.
items.answer:  (C) iron The Second Urbanisation saw a significant technological advancement with the perfection and widespread adoption of iron metallurgy. Iron tools improved agriculture and iron weapons transformed warfare, contributing to societal changes.

items.stem: What were the earliest Indian coins, typically made of silver and bearing stamped symbols, called?
items.answer:  (C) Punch-marked coins Click Here to Buy book on Amazon CH 04: New Beginnings : Cities and States The first coins used in India, emerging due to growing trade, were made of silver. Symbols were stamped or ‘punched’ onto them, leading to their designation as ‘punch-marked coins’ by numismatists and historians.

items.stem: The emergence of new schools of thought like Buddhism and Jainism during the age of mahajanapadas indicates what about the society?

options.label: A
options.text: A period of intellectual and spiritual exploration

options.label: B
options.text: A complete rejection of all older traditions

options.label: C
options.text: A society focused solely on warfare needs

options.label: D
options.text: A decline in trade and urban activities

items.answer:  (A) A period of intellectual and spiritual exploration The rise of new philosophical and religious schools such as Buddhism and Jainism during this era signifies a time of profound intellectual ferment and spiritual seeking, with diverse ideas about life and ethics being discussed.

items.stem: Which of the following was NOT one of the four varnas in the social system that emerged from Vedic texts?
items.answer:  (D) Antyajas (outcastes or untouchables) The varna system, originating from Vedic texts, comprised four categories : Brahmins (knowledge, rituals), Kshatriyas (defense, warfare), Vaishyas (trade, agriculture), and Shudras (artisans, service). Those excluded from this system were later termed differently.

items.stem: All of the following were typical functions or characteristics of a raja in a monarchical mahajanapada EXCEPT :

options.label: A
options.text: Collecting taxes or revenue from people

options.label: B
options.text: Maintaining an army for defense or war

options.label: C
options.text: Being directly elected by all adult citizens

options.label: D
options.text: Getting fortifications built around the capital

items.answer:  (C) Being directly elected by all adult citizens In monarchical mahajanapadas, the raja’s position was usually hereditary. While they collected taxes, maintained armies, and built forts, direct election by all citizens was a feature of some gana- sanghas, not typical monarchies.

items.stem: Which of the following pairs correctly matches a mahajanapada with its approximate geographical location in present-day India?
items.answer:  (C) Avanti - Central India Avanti was a powerful mahajanapada located in the region of present-day Madhya Pradesh in central India. Gandhara was in the northwest, Magadha in eastern India (Bihar), and Kuru in northern India.

items.stem: Assertion (A) : Iron tools and weapons became widespread during the Second Urbanisation, impacting agriculture and warfare. Reason (R) : The techniques for extracting and shaping iron were first discovered during the Harappan civilization. explanation of A. correct explanation of A.

items.answer:  (C) A is true, but R is false Iron metallurgy became widespread during the Second Urbanisation, improving agriculture and warfare. However, the Harappan civilization was primarily known for copper and bronze; iron techniques were perfected later, from the early 2nd millennium BCE.

items.stem: Which of the following pairings of a term and its description related to ancient Indian society is INCORRECT? clan

items.answer:  (C) Jati - Social group based on religious belief A jati was primarily a community or group of people with a specific professional occupation, and the skills were often passed down generations, not defined by religious belief. Varna, janapada, and sabha are correctly described. NODIA

items.stem: Some mahajanapadas like Vajji had democratic elements in their governance. Which of the above statements is/are correct?
items.answer:  (B) 3 only Most mahajanapada capitals were large, well-fortified cities. Iron metallurgy was a major technological shift during the Second Urbanisation. However, states like Vajji (a gana or sangha) indeed exhibited democratic features.

items.stem: A trader in ancient India regularly travels along a major route connecting the northwestern regions, through the Ganga plains, all the way to eastern India, exchanging goods like textiles and spices. Which major ancient trade route is this trader most likely using for travel?
items.answer:  (C) The Uttarapatha route The Uttarapatha was a crucial ancient trade route that connected the northwestern parts of the Indian subcontinent with the Ganga plains and extended towards eastern India. It was vital for trade and cultural exchange across these regions.

items.stem: In the varna system, the Vaishyas were primarily supposed to increase society’s wealth through occupations like trade, business, or _____.
items.answer:  (D) agriculture The Vaishya varna was traditionally associated with economic activities aimed at generating wealth for society. Their primary occupations included trade, business, and also agriculture, playing a key role in production and commerce.

items.stem: What was the primary role of the Kshatriya varna in ancient Indian society?

options.label: A
options.text: To preserve and spread sacred knowledge well

options.label: B
options.text: To engage in trade and manage commerce

options.label: C
options.text: To defend society and land, engage warfare

options.label: D
options.text: To perform artisanal work and offer service

items.answer:  (C) To defend society and land, engage warfare The Kshatriya varna was traditionally tasked with the protection of society and its territory. This involved roles in governance, military leadership, and engaging in warfare when necessary to maintain order and security.

items.stem: Around what time did cities begin to emerge in the southern regions of the Indian subcontinent, marking urbanization ?
items.answer:  (C) Around 400 BCE While urbanization was prominent in northern India earlier, cities in the southern regions of the subcontinent started emerging from about 400 BCE. This period also saw the rise of southern kingdoms like the Cholas, Cheras, and Pandyas.

items.stem: The existence of fortifications and moats around mahajanapada capitals suggests what about the political climate of that era?

options.label: A
options.text: A period of complete peace and no conflict

options.label: B
options.text: A need for defense against potential attacks

options.label: C
options.text: A focus purely on religious and ceremonial

options.label: D
options.text: A lack of organized military structures

items.answer:  (B) A need for defense against potential attacks The construction of strong fortifications and defensive moats around major cities indicates that these urban centers faced potential threats. This implies a political environment where warfare or raids between states were possibilities, necessitating robust defenses. Downloaded from www.pdf.tube CH 04: New Beginnings : Cities and States

items.stem: How did the use of iron differ between the First Urbanisation (Harappan) and the Second Urbanisation in India?

options.label: A
options.text: Iron was dominant in First; bronze in Second

options.label: B
options.text: Iron was absent in First; widespread in Second

options.label: C
options.text: Both used iron equally for all tools

options.label: D
options.text: Bronze was absent in Second; iron in First

items.answer:  (B) Iron was absent in First; widespread in Second The Harappan Civilization (First Urbanisation) was primarily a bronze-age culture, with copper and bronze being the main metals for tools and artifacts. The Second Urbanisation saw the widespread adoption and mastery of iron technology.

items.stem: Which of the following correctly pairs an ancient Indian region/city with its significant characteristic during the period of mahajanapadas? - Capital of Magadha mahajanapada India settlement

Vajji was a republic, Takshashila was in Gandhara, and Kaushambi was a major capital.

items.stem: The Dakshinapatha trade route started from Kaushambi and crossed the _____ Range of hills to proceed southwards.
items.answer:  (C) Vindhya The Dakshinapatha, a major ancient southern trade route, originated from Kaushambi (near Prayagraj) and traversed the Vindhya Range to connect with regions in southern India, facilitating trade and cultural exchange.

items.stem: In the context of ancient Indian governance, what was a ‘sabha’ or ‘samiti’?

options.label: A

options.label: B
options.text: An assembly or council for discussing matters

options.label: C
options.text: A military outpost on the kingdom’s frontier

options.label: D
options.text: A school for training young princes, chiefs

items.answer:  (B) An assembly or council for discussing matters A ‘sabha’ or ‘samiti’ in a janapada or mahajanapada was an assembly or council where matters concerning the clan or state were discussed. The raja was often expected to consider their advice in governance.

items.stem: “Which mahajanapada in central India marked the southern extent of the 16 mahajanapadas, stretching from Gandhara in the northwest to Anga in the east?”
items.answer:  (C) Ashmaka The traditional list of sixteen mahajanapadas covered a vast geographical area, stretching from Gandhara in the northwest, Anga in the east, and extending to Ashmaka located in central India, near the Godavari River.

items.stem: The gradual reorganization of regional cultures into janapadas was often based on clans sharing common language and what other factor?
items.answer:  (B) Common customs and traditions held Janapadas typically formed as clans or groups of people, likely sharing not only a common language but also common customs and traditions, which helped forge a collective identity and territorial association over the time. NODIA

items.stem: Which of the following was NOT a significant impact of the development of iron metallurgy during the Second Urbanisation?

options.label: A
options.text: Facilitation of agriculture on a larger scale

options.label: B
options.text: Creation of lighter and sharper weapons

options.label: C
options.text: The decline of all trade and commerce

items.answer:  (C) The decline of all trade and commerce Iron metallurgy significantly boosted agriculture and warfare capabilities. It did not cause a decline in trade; rather, growing urban centers and states likely fostered more complex trade networks during this period of urbanization.

items.stem: The ancient trade route connecting northwestern regions to the Ganga plains and eastern India was known as the _____.
items.answer:  (C) Uttarapatha The Uttarapatha was a major ancient northern trade route that facilitated commerce and cultural interactions by connecting the northwestern parts of the Indian subcontinent with the Gangetic plains and further east.

items.answer:  (C) The Harappan Civilization’s First Urbanisation The Indus Valley/Harappan Civilization, known as India’s First Urbanisation, was characterized by sophisticated urban planning, including writing systems, sanitation, and a society with diverse specialized occupations.

items.stem: A historian is studying an ancient Indian state where the ruler was selected by an assembly, and major decisions were taken through discussion and voting rather than by a hereditary monarch. This state would most likely be classified as which of these?

items.answer:  (B) A gana or sangha (early republic) States like Vajji and Malla, referred to as ganas or sanghas, had political systems where assemblies held significant power, including the selection of the ruler and decision-making through discussion, fitting the description of an early republic.

items.stem: The fortification of mahajanapada capitals with walls and moats suggests an emphasis on what aspect?
items.answer:  (D) Defense and security The construction of strong defensive structures like walls and moats around the capitals of mahajanapadas indicates a significant concern for defense and security, suggesting a period where protection from external threats was crucial.

items.stem: The introduction of _____ coins, made by stamping symbols onto metal, marked an important development in trade during this period.
items.answer:  (C) punch-marked silver The advent of coinage was a significant innovation for facilitating trade. The earliest Indian coins were typically made of silver and had symbols ‘punched’ onto them, hence they are known as punch-marked coins.

items.answer:  (C) The Vindhya Range hills The Vindhya Range historically served as a geographical divider between northern and southern India. Trade routes like the Dakshinapatha, connecting the Ganga plains to the south, had to traverse these hills.

items.stem: The two major ancient Indian trade routes mentioned that connected different parts of the subcontinent were the Uttarapatha and the _____.

items.answer:  (B) Iron Metallurgy - Improved agriculture and weapons. The widespread adoption of iron metallurgy was a key technological development during the Second Urbanisation. Iron tools enhanced agricultural productivity, and iron weapons provided a military advantage. Bronze was key to the First Urbanisation. Coinage was for trade.

items.stem: An ancient settlement shows evidence of regularly held assemblies where clan elders discussed important matters and even had a say in the selection of their leader. This settlement most likely belonged to which type of political entity in ancient India?

options.label: A
options.text: A province of a large, centralized empire

options.label: B
options.text: A janapada or a gana-sangha mahajanapada

options.label: C
options.text: A purely nomadic pastoral community group

options.label: D
options.text: A small, isolated monastic religious order

items.answer:  (B) A janapada or a gana-sangha mahajanapada Janapadas were characterized by assemblies (sabha or samiti) where clan matters were discussed, and the raja consulted these bodies. Some mahajanapadas, known as gana-sanghas, had even more powerful assemblies involved in selecting rulers.

items.stem: Which of these was NOT a primary reason for the disintegration of the Indus/Harappan Civilization (First Urbanisation)?

options.label: A
options.text: Abandonment of some of its major cities

options.label: B
options.text: Disappearance of its complex urban order

options.label: C
options.text: The widespread adoption of iron technology

options.label: D
options.text: Reversion to a more rural or village lifestyle

items.answer:  (C) The widespread adoption of iron technology The decline of the Harappan Civilization involved the abandonment of cities and the loss of its urban characteristics. The widespread adoption of iron technology was a feature of the much later Second Urbanisation, not a cause of Harappan decline. NODIA CH 04: New Beginnings : Cities and States

items.stem: The fertile plains of which two major rivers were central to the Second Urbanisation in India?
items.answer:  (C) Ganga and Indus rivers The Second Urbanisation predominantly flourished in the fertile plains of the Ganga River and parts of the Indus (Sindhu) basin, along with neighboring regions, providing the agricultural base for growing populations and urban centers.

items.stem: In the context of the varna system, what was the general expectation for the Shudra varna? trade

options.label: A

options.label: B
options.text: To hold the highest positions in governance

options.label: C
options.text: To serve as priests and perform rituals

options.label: D
options.text: To be artisans, craftspeople, or provide service

items.answer:  (D) To be artisans, craftspeople, or provide service The Shudra varna was generally expected to provide labor, service, and artisanal skills to the other varnas within the societal framework, contributing through various forms of manual work and crafts.

items.stem: The period of the Second Urbanisation saw the emergence of important religious and philosophical schools of thought, including late Vedic, Buddhist, and _____ traditions.
items.answer:  (C) Jain Alongside late Vedic thought and the rise of Buddhism, Jainism also emerged as a significant religious and philosophical tradition during this transformative period of the Second Urbanisation in ancient India, contributing to its diverse intellectual landscape.

items.stem: The interconnectedness of the Indian subcontinent by 300-200 BCE through trade routes facilitated the movement of goods and what else? raw materials for weapon production

options.label: A
options.text: Only military troops and their supplies

options.label: B
options.text: Primarily wild animals for royal entertainment

options.label: C
options.text: People, ideas, and cultural teachings too

items.answer:  (C) People, ideas, and cultural teachings too The extensive network of trade routes not only enabled the exchange of goods but also facilitated the movement of people, leading to the spread of ideas, religious teachings, cultural practices, and technological knowledge across different regions.

items.stem: A ruler in ancient India establishes a new city. To ensure its prosperity and sustainability, the ruler focuses on cultivable land, mines, timber, good pastures, reliable water sources (not solely rain-dependent), and good roads. This approach aligns with the principles of statecraft advocated by whom?

options.label: B

options.label: D
options.text: Ashoka in his rock edicts known

items.answer:  (C) Kautilya in the Arthashastra text Kautilya, in the Arthashastra, emphasizes the importance of a well-endowed territory with resources like cultivable land, mines, forests, pastures, reliable water, and good infrastructure (roads, waterways) for a kingdom’s prosperity and strength. items.stem: Which of these ancient Indian sites is INCORRECTLY paired with its primary association? learning (Implied as a center of learning, often Buddhist) outpost
items.answer:  (D) Shishupalgarh - A minor Harappan trading outpost Shishupalgarh was a major fortified urban center in eastern India, the capital of Kalinga, flourishing during the Second Urbanisation, not a Harappan site. The other pairings are appropriate for that period.

items.stem: Assertion (A) : The Second Urbanisation in India was marked by the emergence of fortified cities and the use of coinage. Reason (R) : These developments were driven by a decline in agricultural production and long- distance trade in India. explanation of A. correct explanation of A.

options.label: B
options.text: Both A and R are true, but R is not the

options.label: C
options.text: A is true, but R is false

options.label: D
options.text: A is false, but R is true

items.answer:  (C) A is true, but R is false The Second Urbanisation did see fortified cities and the introduction of coinage. However, these were generally supported by advancements in agriculture (like iron ploughs) and flourishing trade networks, not a decline in them.

items.stem: Changing one’s professional occupation was completely impossible in early periods. Which of the above statements is/are correct usually?
items.answer:  (A) 2 only The varna system had four main categories. Jatis indeed could have sub-jatis with their own customs. While it became rigid, evidence suggests some occupational flexibility in earlier periods.

items.stem: What does ‘metallurgy’ refer to? metals

options.label: D
options.text: The science and technology of extracting

items.answer:  (D) The science and technology of extracting metals Metallurgy is the branch of science and technology concerned with the properties of metals and their production and purification, including the extraction of metals from their ores and shaping them into useful objects or tools.

items.stem: Which of the following was one of the most powerful mahajanapadas located in the region of present-day Bihar?
items.answer:  (C) Magadha Magadha, with its capital at Rajagriha (and later Pataliputra), was one of the most powerful and influential mahajanapadas, situated in the area of modern-day Bihar in eastern India. NODIA CH 04: New Beginnings : Cities and States

items.stem: The mention of guilds (shrenis) of traders and craftspeople in ancient texts suggests what about the economic organization of the time?

options.label: A

options.label: B
options.text: There was a high degree of organization

options.label: C
options.text: Barter was the only method of exchange

options.label: D
options.text: Craft production was limited to rural areas

items.answer:  (B) There was a high degree of organization The existence of guilds (shrenis) indicates that traders and craftspeople were organizing themselves into associations. This suggests a relatively sophisticated level of economic organization, cooperation, and regulation within these professional groups.

items.stem: How did the geographical focus of the First Urbanisation (Harappan) differ from that of the Second Urbanisation in India?

options.label: A
options.text: First was south; Second was far north

options.label: B
options.text: First was Indus basin; Second was Ganga

options.label: C
options.text: First was east coast; Second was in west

options.label: D
options.text: Both were focused solely on Deccan area

items.answer:  (B) First was Indus basin; Second was Ganga The First Urbanisation, the Harappan Civilization, was centered around the Indus River basin and the Sarasvati River. The Second Urbanisation saw its primary development in the fertile plains of the Ganga River and adjacent regions.

items.stem: Which term is correctly defined in the context of ancient Indian states?

options.label: A

items.answer:  (C) Raja - The hereditary or selected ruler/chief ‘Raja’ was the term used for the ruler or chief of a janapada or mahajanapada. This position could be hereditary in monarchies or filled through selection/election in some republican states (gana-sanghas).

items.stem: A group of artisans in an ancient Indian city specializes in making high-quality iron swords and agricultural tools. Their products are in demand both locally and in neighboring territories. This scenario best reflects the technological advancements of which period?
items.answer:  (D) The Second Urbanisation (Iron Age) The specialization in crafting high-quality iron swords and agricultural tools points to the Iron Age and the period of the Second Urbanisation in India. During this time, iron metallurgy became widespread, significantly impacting various aspects of life.

items.stem: Which of these was NOT a common feature of the capitals of the mahajanapadas? villages too

items.answer:  (A) They were usually small, undefended rural villages The capitals of the mahajanapadas were typically large, well-fortified cities that served as centers of political administration and power, not small, undefended villages. They were designed for defense and governance.

items.stem: The city of Ujjayini was the capital of which prominent mahajanapada in central India?
items.answer:  (D) Avanti Ujjayini (modern Ujjain) was an important city and the capital of the Avanti mahajanapada, which was a significant power in central India during the period of the sixteen mahajanapadas.

items.answer:  (C) Monarchies had hereditary rule; gana-sanghas had assemblies Monarchical mahajanapadas typically had hereditary rulers (rajas) who, while advised by councils, held ultimate authority. Gana-sanghas had assemblies (sabha/samiti) that played a more direct role in governance and often in selecting leaders.

items.answer:  (C) The era of the Mahajanapadas/Second Urbanisation The presence of punch-marked silver coins (often without inscriptions initially), iron weaponry, and evidence of large-scale agriculture are all characteristic features of the period of the Mahajanapadas and the Second Urbanisation in ancient India. MAT CHING TYPE QUESTION 

items.stem: What term is used for the urbanisation that began in the Ganga plains in the 1st millennium BCE?
items.answer:  Second Urbanisation of India.

items.stem: Name one type of ancient literature that provides information about the Second Urbanisation.
items.answer:  Late Vedic/Buddhist/Jain literature (any one).

items.stem: What does the Sanskrit word ‘janapada’ literally mean?
items.answer:  Where the people (jana) have set foot (pada)/settled down.

items.stem: Who was the leader or ruler of a janapada?
items.answer:  Raja.

items.stem: What were the larger states formed by the merger of janapadas called?
items.answer:  Mahajanapadas.

items.stem: How many mahajanapadas are frequently mentioned in ancient texts?
items.answer:  Sixteen.

items.stem: Name one of the four most powerful mahajanapadas mentioned.
items.answer:  Magadha/Kosala/Vatsa/Avanti (any one).

items.stem: What defensive feature, often filled with water, surrounded the fortifications of mahajanapada capitals?
items.answer:  Moat.

items.stem: What was the assembly or council in a janapada called?
items.answer:  Sabha or samiti.

items.stem: In monarchical mahajanapadas, how was the position of the raja usually decided?
items.answer:  It was hereditary (passed from father to son).

items.stem: Name one mahajanapada that functioned as a gana or sangha (republic).
items.answer:  Vajji (or Vrijji)/Malla (any one).

items.stem: How was the raja selected in a gana or sangha?
items.answer:  By the members of the assembly (sabha/samiti).

items.stem: Which metal’s metallurgy became widespread during the Second Urbanisation?
items.answer:  Iron.

items.stem: What innovation related to trade first appeared in India during this period?
items.answer:  Coins.

items.stem: What were the earliest Indian coins, often made of silver, called?
items.answer:  Punch-marked coins.

items.stem: What term refers to a group or community with a specific professional occupation, often passed down generations?
items.answer:  Jati.

items.stem: How many varnas were there according to the Vedic concept?
items.answer:  Four.

items.stem: Which varna was associated with preserving knowledge and performing rituals?
items.answer:  Brahmins.

items.stem: Which varna was expected to defend society and engage in warfare?
items.answer:  Kshatriyas. Downloaded from www.pdf.tube CH 04: New Beginnings : Cities and States

items.stem: Which varna was associated with trade, business, and agriculture?
items.answer:  Vaishyas.

items.stem: Which varna included artisans, craftspeople, workers, or servants?
items.answer:  Shudras.

items.stem: What was the name of the major trade route connecting Northwest India to the Ganga plains?
items.answer:  Uttarapatha.

items.stem: What was the name of the major trade route connecting the Ganga plains to the South?
items.answer:  Dakshinapatha.

items.stem: Name one of the three kingdoms that emerged in South India around 400 BCE.
items.answer:  Cholas/Cheras/Pandyas (any one).

items.answer:  Shishupalgarh (Sisupalgarh). SSHORT Answer QUESTIO 

items.stem: What were the key features of urban life that disappeared after the First Urbanisation (Harappan)?
items.answer:  Elaborate structures, busy markets, specialized occupations, a writing system, sanitation systems, administration, and a state structure with a ruling class disappeared, leading to a rural lifestyle.

items.stem: How do archaeologists and ancient literature help us understand the Second Urbanisation?
items.answer:  Archaeology uncovers physical evidence of ancient cities (fortifications, structures, artifacts). Ancient literature (Vedic, Buddhist, Jain) contains descriptions and references to these new urban centres, their rulers, and life within them.

items.stem: Explain the process by which janapadas likely formed.
items.answer:  People likely formed clans sharing common language and customs. These clans settled in specific territories (janapadas), each led by a ruler (raja) and guided by an assembly (sabha/samiti).

items.stem: Why were the Ganga plains a favourable region for the rise of mahajanapadas?
items.answer:  The fertile plains supported agricultural growth, nearby hills provided iron ore essential for tools and weapons, and expanding trade networks connected different settlements, facilitating growth and state formation.

items.stem: Describe the typical fortifications of a mahajanapada capital city.
items.answer:  Capitals were usually well-fortified with rampart walls, often surrounded by a deep, water-filled moat for extra defense. Gateways were sometimes kept narrow for better control over entry and exit.

items.stem: What was the role of the sabha or samiti in the governance of a janapada?
items.answer:  The sabha/samiti was an assembly, likely of clan elders, where matters concerning the clan were discussed. The raja was expected to consult this assembly before making important decisions.

items.stem: How did governance in monarchical mahajanapadas like Magadha differ from that in ganas/sanghas like Vajji?
items.answer:  In monarchies, the raja held ultimate authority (often hereditary), collected taxes, and maintained an army. In ganas/sanghas, the assembly held more power, making decisions collectively and even selecting the ruler. NODIA

items.stem: Why are ganas/sanghas sometimes called ‘early republics’?
items.answer:  They are called early republics because major decisions, including the selection of the ruler, were made by an assembly through discussion and voting, resembling democratic processes rather than hereditary monarchy.

items.stem: How did the widespread use of iron tools impact agriculture during this period?
items.answer:  Iron tools, being stronger and more efficient than earlier materials, likely facilitated clearing forests and cultivating the fertile but sometimes heavy soil of the Ganga plains more effectively, enabling larger-scale agriculture.

items.stem: Explain the significance of iron in warfare during the time of mahajanapadas.
items.answer:  Iron weapons (swords, spears, arrows) were sharper and possibly lighter or stronger than bronze ones. This technological advantage likely played a role in conflicts and military campaigns between neighbouring mahajanapadas.

items.stem: Why did the introduction of coins become necessary during this period?
items.answer:  As trade networks expanded between janapadas and mahajanapadas, a standardized medium of exchange was needed to facilitate transactions more easily than barter, leading to the first use of coins.

items.stem: Describe the characteristics of the earliest Indian coins.
items.answer:  The first Indian coins were ‘punch-marked coins’, usually made of silver. Symbols representing the issuing authority or region were stamped or ‘punched’ onto the metal pieces.

items.stem: Explain the concept of ‘jati’ in the context of ancient Indian society.
items.answer:  Jati referred to a community or group primarily defined by a specific professional occupation (like potters, weavers, farmers). These skills were typically passed down within the group generationally.

items.stem: Outline the roles associated with the four varnas (Brahmin, Kshatriya, Vaishya, Shudra).
items.answer:  Brahmins dealt with knowledge/rituals; Kshatriyas with defense/governance; Vaishyas with wealth creation (trade, agriculture); Shudras with service, crafts, and labour.

items.stem: Was the varna-jati system always rigid? Explain.
items.answer:  No, In earlier periods, the system was more flexible, with historical evidence showing individuals or communities sometimes changing occupations due to circumstances like drought or migration.

items.stem: What potential negative consequence of the varna-jati system is mentioned?
items.answer:  Over time, the system became rigid and led to social inequalities and discrimination against lower jatis or communities excluded from the main varna structure.

items.stem: What was the significance of the Uttarapatha and Dakshinapatha routes?
items.answer:  These were major ancient routes facilitating trade, travel, pilgrimage, and military movements. Uttarapatha connected the northwest to the east, while Dakshinapatha linked the north to the south, promoting interconnectedness.

items.stem: Describe the city plan of Shishupalgarh.
items.answer:  Shishupalgarh, capital of Kalinga, followed a strict square ground plan. It had imposing fortifications, broad streets, and controlled gateways, indicating sophisticated urban planning.

items.stem: What resources made the southern kingdoms (Cholas, Cheras, Pandyas) important trade centres?
items.answer:  The southern regions were rich in resources like precious and semi-precious stones, gold, and spices, which were highly valued in trade both within India and overseas. Click Here to Buy book on Amazon CH 04: New Beginnings : Cities and States

items.stem: Compare the primary metal used in the First Urbanisation (Harappan) with the key metal of the Second Urbanisation.
items.answer:  The First Urbanisation primarily utilized copper and bronze metallurgy. The Second Urbanisation saw the widespread adoption and mastery of iron metallurgy.

items.stem: How did the political landscape change by around 300 BCE ?
items.answer:  By around 300 BCE, the era of the independent mahajanapadas was ending, paving the way for new political developments, likely larger empires that consolidated these regions.

items.stem: What evidence suggests warfare occurred between mahajanapadas?
items.answer:  The development of better iron weapons and notes evidence of military campaigns between neighbouring mahajanapadas, alongside alliances, suggesting conflict was a factor.

items.stem: How were skills typically passed on within a jati?
items.answer:  Skills defining a jati, such as metallurgy, pottery, weaving, or farming techniques, were generally transmitted from one generation to the next within the community or family.

items.stem: What does the existence of fortified cities suggest about the mahajanapada period?
items.answer:  Fortified cities suggest concerns about security and defense. They imply the existence of organized states capable of mobilizing resources for large constructions and indicate potential threats from rivals or invaders.

items.stem: Besides governance and social structure, what other major developments occurred during the age of mahajanapadas?
items.answer:  This era saw the emergence of new philosophical/ religious schools (Buddhism, Jainism), advancements in iron technology, the introduction of coinage, and the expansion of trade networks across the subcontinent. LONG ANSWER QUESTIO 

items.stem: Analyse Kautilya’s description of an ideal kingdom (quoted at the start). What aspects focus on security, economy, and resources?
items.answer:  Kautilya emphasizes security through fortifications (capital, frontiers). Economically, he stresses productivity, diverse commodities, good roads/ waterways for trade. Resource-wise, he highlights the need for sustainable land (agriculture, pastures), mines, forests (timber, elephants), and reliable water sources not solely dependent on rain, ensuring self-sufficiency and resilience.

items.stem: Compare and contrast the political systems of monarchical mahajanapadas (like Magadha) and republican ganas/sanghas (like Vajji).
items.answer:  Monarchies had hereditary rulers (rajas) with ultimate authority, supported by ministers/ assemblies, focused on tax collection and military power. Ganas/sanghas vested more power in the assembly, which made key decisions, including selecting the ruler, functioning more democratically or oligarchically rather than through single, hereditary rule.

items.stem: Compare and contrast the administrative structures and decision-making processes of monarchical states like Magadha and republican states like the Vajji confederacy in ancient India.
items.answer:  Monarchies like Magadha had centralized rule with a hereditary king holding supreme power, aided by ministers. Decisions were mostly top- down. In contrast, republican states like Vajji were governed by assemblies of elders who made decisions collectively, with leadership chosen rather than inherited.

items.stem: Analyse the potential reasons why the Second Urbanisation flourished specifically in the Ganga plains.
items.answer:  The fertile alluvial soil supported surplus agriculture, feeding larger populations. Abundant iron ore nearby enabled advanced tools and weapons. The Ganga river system facilitated trade and communication. The rise of new religious and NODIA philosophical ideas also stimulated intellectual and social activity conducive to urban growth.

items.stem: “The introduction of iron metallurgy was a key catalyst for the Second Urbanisation.” Evaluate this statement.
items.answer:  Iron tools likely boosted agricultural productivity (clearing land, better ploughs), supporting larger populations needed for cities. Iron weapons enhanced military capabilities, aiding state formation and consolidation by powerful mahajanapadas. Therefore, iron metallurgy was crucial, enabling the resource base and political stability required for urbanisation.

items.stem: Analyse the function of the varna-jati system in organizing ancient Indian society. What were its strengths and weaknesses?
items.answer:  It structured society by defining roles and occupations (varna) and organizing communities based on livelihood skills (jati), providing social order and facilitating economic specialization. Its strength was stability and skill transmission. Its weakness was increasing rigidity over time, leading to hereditary hierarchy, inequality, and discrimination.

items.stem: Explain how the development of trade routes like Uttarapatha and Dakshinapatha contributed to the interconnectedness of the Indian subcontinent.
items.answer:  These major arteries linked diverse regions from the northwest to the east (Uttarapatha) and north to south (Dakshinapatha). They facilitated the movement not just of goods (trade) but also people (travelers, pilgrims, armies) and ideas (religious teachings, cultural practices), weaving the subcontinent into a more integrated network.

items.stem: Compare the timeline and geographical focus of the First Urbanisation (Harappan) and the Second Urbanisation.
items.answer:  The First Urbanisation peaked earlier (c. 2600- 1900 BCE) primarily in the Indus-Sarasvati river basins (northwest). The Second Urbanisation began much later (c. 7th-6th centuries BCE onwards) mainly in the Ganga plains, eventually spreading across large parts of North, Central, East, and later South India.

items.stem: How might the rise of new religious and philosophical schools (Buddhism, Jainism) have influenced society during the Second Urbanisation?
items.answer:  These schools often challenged existing social norms and religious practices (like aspects of the Vedic tradition or the rigidity of varna). Their emphasis on ethics, non-violence, and alternative paths to liberation likely attracted diverse followers, potentially fostering social change and contributing to the period’s intellectual vibrancy.

items.stem: Analyse the statement : “Most of the ancient capitals of the mahajanapadas continue to be living cities today.” What does this imply?
items.answer:  This implies remarkable continuity of settlement and strategic importance. Locations chosen 2500 years ago often remained favourable for trade, administration, or resources over millennia. It highlights the deep historical roots of many modern Indian cities and the enduring nature of certain geographical advantages.

items.stem: Discuss the role of trade in the prosperity of the mahajanapadas and the later southern kingdoms.
items.answer:  Trade was vital. For mahajanapadas, expanding trade networks facilitated growth and interaction. Coinage emerged to support this. Southern kingdoms profited immensely from trading valuable local resources (gems, gold, spices) both within India via routes like Dakshinapatha and overseas, contributing significantly to their wealth and influence.

items.stem: What does the reference to Kautilya’s Arthashastra at the beginning suggest about the concerns of statecraft during this era?
items.answer:  It suggests sophisticated thinking about state management. Concerns included security (fortification), economic prosperity (resources, trade, infrastructure), self-sufficiency (water, food), population welfare (sustaining people during calamities), and maintaining order – reflecting a well-developed understanding of practical governance principles. Downloaded from www.pdf.tube CH 04: New Beginnings : Cities and States

items.stem: Why was the ability for individuals or communities to change occupations (as mentioned regarding the early varna-jati system) important for societal resilience?
items.answer:  Flexibility allowed society to adapt to changing circumstances. If a drought ruined farming, communities could shift to crafts or trade in cities. If Brahmins were needed for trade or military roles, they could adapt. This adaptability helped society cope with calamities and evolving needs, enhancing overall resilience.

items.stem: Analyse the potential relationship between increased agricultural production (enabled by iron tools) and state formation (mahajanapadas).
items.answer:  Surplus agriculture, enabled by iron tools, could support larger, denser populations and non- farming specialists (soldiers, administrators, craftspeople). This surplus could be taxed by rulers (rajas) to fund armies, build fortifications, and manage larger territories, directly contributing to the formation and consolidation of states (mahajanapadas).

items.stem: Considering the evidence, evaluate whether the Second Urbanisation represented a complete break from the past or incorporated earlier traditions.
items.answer:  It wasn’t a complete break. While distinct from the Harappan civilisation, it built upon earlier foundations. Concepts like sabha/samiti originated in Vedic times. Iron technology developed gradually over preceding centuries. The Second Urbanisation represented a new phase integrating technological advancements, evolving social structures, and new ideas onto existing cultural layers. CASE BASED QUESTIO 

items.stem: Archaeologists excavate a site in the Ganga plains dating to the 6th century BCE. They find remnants of mud-brick houses, iron sickles and ploughshares, pottery shards, and numerous silver punch-marked coins featuring symbols like hills and trees. They find no evidence of large fortifications or monumental buildings. (i) Based on the findings, would this site more likely represent a large mahajanapada capital or a smaller settlement within a janapada/ mahajanapada? (ii) What do the iron tools suggest about the economy of this settlement? (iii) What does the presence of numerous punch- marked coins indicate?
items.answer:  (i) It likely represents a smaller settlement or prosperous village, possibly within a janapada/mahajanapada, rather than a major fortified capital, due to the lack of large fortifications or monumental structures. (ii) The iron sickles and ploughshares strongly suggest an economy based significantly on agriculture, using advanced tools for cultivation in the fertile plains. (iii) The coins indicate active participation in trade and a monetized economy. It suggests the settlement was connected to wider trade networks where goods were exchanged using currency, moving beyond simple barter.

items.stem: A traveller’s account from the 5th century BCE describes visiting Vaishali, the capital of the Vajji confederacy. The account mentions large assembly halls where representatives from different clans met frequently to discuss state matters, elect leaders for specific tasks, and vote on important decisions by using marked wooden sticks. (i) What type of political system does this account describe for Vajji? (ii) How does this system differ from the governance likely found in Magadha at the same time? (iii) What aspect of this account points towards early democratic practices?
items.answer:  (i) This describes a republican or oligarchic system, specifically a gana or sangha, where decisions were made collectively by an assembly rather than by a single hereditary monarch. (ii) Magadha was likely a monarchy where the raja held supreme power, inherited the throne, and made decisions with ministers, unlike Vajji’s system of collective decision- making and elected leadership within the assembly. (iii) The practice of representatives meeting, discussing state matters, electing leaders, NODIA and voting on decisions using marked sticks are clear indicators of early democratic or republican processes of governance.

items.stem: A community of potters (a specific jati) living in a janapada faces hardship after their clay source is depleted. The local raja needs more soldiers for his army due to conflict with a neighbour. Some young men from the potter community consider joining the army. (i) According to the traditional varna system, which varna was primarily associated with warfare? (ii) Based on historical discussions of social flexibility, could these men from a potter jati (likely considered Shudra or Vaishya depending on context) potentially join the army? (iii) Evaluate the potential social implications if they successfully become soldiers.
items.answer:  (i) The Kshatriya varna was traditionally associated with warfare and defending society. (ii) Yes, In earlier periods, the system had flexibility, and individuals or groups could change occupations due to circumstances, implying they might have been able to join the army. (iii) Successfully becoming soldiers might offer them better economic prospects and potentially elevate their social standing, challenging the rigidity of associating jati solely with a specific, inherited occupation, reflecting the system’s earlier adaptability.

items.stem: Traders based in Ujjayini (capital of Avanti) want to transport goods like textiles and iron tools to ports on the western coast and also establish connections with kingdoms in the south known for spices and gems. (i) Which major trade route would likely be used to connect Ujjayini to the southern kingdoms? (ii) What kinds of goods might these traders hope to acquire from the south? (iii) Evaluate the importance of such trade for the economy of Avanti.
items.answer:  (i) They would likely utilize parts of the Dakshinapatha route, which connected the northern plains (via cities like Kaushambi, possibly linking to Ujjayini) southwards across the Vindhyas. (ii) They would hope to acquire valuable resources mentioned as available in the south, such as spices, precious stones (gems), and possibly gold. (iii) This trade would be very important. Exporting local goods (textiles, tools) and importing valuable southern resources would boost Avanti’s economy, increase wealth, and strengthen its position as a major hub connecting different regions.
